chapter: Billy Phillips, George Jones and the Shriners trip
title: The Shriners trip to Indianapolis
summary: Dawson went with Jones's band to Indianapolis via Memphis in costume, expenses paid, with his tenor banjo a novelty there.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Went with the shrines. I went to Indianapolis with him. I took my tenor banjo that, uh, when I, when I went up there, there people were surprised. They had never seen him, had never seen a tenor banjo up there before. Yeah? Oh. And, uh, I, uh, he had, he had this, this fellow called Snow on the guitar, and Jim Dixon, and myself, and Cornelius, that same fellow I told you, with, uh, had a cigarette you put behind his head. And, and the shrines, uh, the shrines hired him. He got, he got us. I was on my vacation. I was working at the bank, and I, I was on my vacation. And, uh, he taken, and, uh, they gave us, uh, them, you know how they, how they, how they, oh, uh, them farmers wear them, uh, overhaul pants. Yeah. And blue, uh, jumpers, you know, jumpers and red handkerchief. Yeah, like that. Around the neck, you see, and them big old sun hats. And they had a couple of big bales of cotton, you see, on the float. And we got to Memphis, we parade all around in Memphis, you see. When we sitting up on the bale of cotton, he was singing, he could sing all them old, old-time songs, you know, like honeysuckle and all that, man. And, uh, we parade all around Memphis, and then we come all back and got in the train, and went all the way to Indianapolis, you see. At, uh, the Panama Limit was the train that went off, and them shrines, all them nobles were in the shrines. They had, uh, I see, I think, uh, uh, this fella, the wine boy, he was portentated at the shrine. Well, they had a carload, nothing, nothing, nothing but liquor in the back. They had a big camel in the back, and they brought the camel and all, and they had, uh, that, that place over there was dry. Indiana was dry. Yeah, they brought their own liquor. And, uh, we just pulled all, it was just like Carnival over there. And as soon as we made the parade in, uh, on Main Street, uh, by the Claypool Hotel, and a girl was way up in one of the hotel windows, she fell out and went and killed herself. Leaned too far over. Yeah. Yeah, it was a first accident in the parade. And we, uh, we paraded all around in Indianapolis, and, uh, and then we went downstairs, they went up, up in, uh, I think about 23 stories high, the Claypool Hotel is. And they went up in, uh, special room up there, and they had the Archbishop, the Bishop was up there with them, you know. The shrine was strong, you know. And, uh, we, uh, down in the basement down there playing on one side we was playing on, and on the other side the Highway and Band was playing on the other side. We had two bands. Ah, we were banding on one side, we were on the other side. Oh, we made plenty money. Uh-huh. We, we, we left here on a Sunday, and we can get back to, like, Friday night. Oh.
And they paid, uh, your way and all your expenses? Oh, yeah, sure. Yeah.
So, everything. And then, you say they've never seen a tenor banjo on there.

No, they never saw a tenor banjo. About what year that was? Oh, let's see. Oh, you got me now. Uh, 17, 19, 17, 19, 18. The time of the First World War, you think? 19, it was right after that, uh, uh, about 1919. Oh, yeah. About 1919, that was. Oh, yeah. Because I, I went, I went to the Whitney in 1917. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Are you still mad by the way?
Yeah, yeah, yeah. All this time, right? Yeah.
Still mad. Right, yeah. Right, yeah.
